clinicalPearls: ALys is a rare autosomal dominant amyloidosis caused by mutations in the lysozyme gene (LYZ).
It is characteristically multi-visceral, with prominent involvement of the kidney, liver, spleen and gastrointestinal tract.
Spontaneous and potentially life-threatening haemorrhage is a hallmark, with reports of hepatic and splenic rupture and gastrointestinal bleeding.
Sicca symptoms of dry eyes and mouth and cutaneous petechiae are recognised features.
Renal involvement is common but often slowly progressive, with nephrotic syndrome developing over years.
Cardiac and neurological involvement are typically mild or absent, which helps distinguish ALys from ATTR.
Diagnosis rests on tissue typing and LYZ sequencing; there is no specific antifibril therapy, so management is supportive and directed at complications.
reference.pathophysiology: Lysozyme is a bacteriolytic enzyme secreted by macrophages, Paneth cells and various epithelia. Amyloidogenic variants destabilise the folded protein, promoting partial unfolding, aggregation and deposition of lysozyme-derived amyloid fibrils in the extracellular matrix of viscera. Deposition is widespread but shows particular avidity for the gastrointestinal tract, liver, spleen and kidney, where infiltration weakens tissue integrity and predisposes to haemorrhage and organ dysfunction. Because lysozyme is produced by many cell types, the amyloid source cannot be removed by transplantation of a single organ, and deposition continues over decades in a slowly progressive fashion.
additionalDifferentials: Other hereditary amyloidoses (fibrinogen, apolipoprotein A-I, transthyretin)
Other causes of gastrointestinal bleeding or hepatosplenomegaly
Sjögren syndrome for the sicca features
additionalInvestigations: Biopsy of affected tissue (gut, liver or kidney) with Congo red staining
Amyloid typing by mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry
Cross-sectional imaging of the liver and spleen to assess size and rupture risk
Full blood count and clotting studies given the bleeding risk
Serum free light chains and immunofixation to exclude AL amyloidosis
redFlags: Acute abdominal pain with haemodynamic compromise suggesting hepatic or splenic rupture
reference.prognosis: The disorder is generally slowly progressive, with survival often measured in decades, but life-threatening visceral haemorrhage from organ rupture is the principal cause of acute mortality.
pitfalls: Mistyping as AL amyloidosis and exposing patients to chemotherapy
Underestimating the risk of spontaneous organ rupture
Attributing sicca symptoms to Sjögren syndrome without considering amyloid
Relying on single-organ transplantation to remove the amyloid source
references: Oxford Textbook of Medicine, chapter on hereditary amyloidosis
International Society of Amyloidosis nomenclature guidelines
management: No single-organ transplant removes the amyloid source, as lysozyme is produced by many cell types, so management is largely supportive and surveillance-based

Vigilant management of spontaneous visceral haemorrhage from hepatic or splenic rupture and gastrointestinal bleeding, with resuscitation, correction of coagulopathy, and interventional radiological embolisation or surgery
Manage renal involvement with renin-angiotensin blockade for proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome, progressing to renal replacement therapy as disease advances
Surveillance cross-sectional imaging of liver and spleen for organomegaly and rupture risk, with advice to avoid contact sports and abdominal trauma
Symptomatic treatment of sicca symptoms with ocular lubricants and saliva substitutes
Multidisciplinary care through a specialist amyloidosis centre spanning haematology, nephrology and gastroenterology
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal dominant LYZ inheritance
